concepts.name: Definition and Constitutional Basis of Simple Majority
key_dimensions: Distinction between simple majority (majority of members present and voting) vs absolute majority vs special majority
Why simple majority amendments are NOT governed by Article 368 — the critical trap
Constitutional provisions that explicitly permit ordinary legislative process for amendments
Implication: simple majority amendments do not require Presidential assent under Article 368 procedure

concepts.name: Article 368 Exclusion: What Falls Outside Its Scope
key_dimensions: Article 368(1) explicitly saves Parliament's constituent power but simple majority provisions bypass this entirely
Judicial interpretation of 'amendment' vs 'legislation' in the context of these provisions
UPSC trap: confusing 'constitutional amendment' with 'change to constitutional text' — not all textual changes need Article 368
Consequence: simple majority amendments cannot be challenged as violating Basic Structure doctrine (debated)

concepts.name: Admission of New States and Formation of New States — Article 2
key_dimensions: Parliament can admit new states or establish new states on such terms as it thinks fit by simple majority
Distinction between Article 2 (new states not part of India) and Article 3 (reorganisation of existing states)
Example: Sikkim's admission in 1975 used Article 2 route initially
Trap: Article 2 requires simple majority; Article 3 also requires simple majority but has additional Presidential recommendation requirement

concepts.name: Alteration of State Boundaries — Article 3 and Its Procedure
key_dimensions: Five types of changes Parliament can make under Article 3: formation, increase, diminish, alter boundaries, alter names
Mandatory Presidential reference to State Legislature for opinion — but Parliament NOT bound by that opinion
Simple majority sufficiency despite affecting federal units — key UPSC controversy point
Comparison with countries like USA where state consent is mandatory — India's 'indestructible Union' principle

concepts.name: Second Schedule Amendments — Salaries and Emoluments
key_dimensions: Second Schedule covers emoluments of President, Governors, Judges of Supreme Court/High Courts, CAG, etc.
Can be amended by simple majority of Parliament
Trap: Judges' salaries are charged to Consolidated Fund of India (non-votable) but the Schedule fixing amounts needs only simple majority to alter
Recent relevance: Changes to salaries of constitutional functionaries done through ordinary legislation

concepts.name: Fifth Schedule Amendments — Scheduled Areas and Tribes
key_dimensions: Parliament can amend Fifth Schedule by simple majority — covers administration of Scheduled Areas
President has power to increase/decrease Scheduled Areas by order under Fifth Schedule Para 6
Trap: Fifth Schedule is amendable by simple majority but PESA Act (1996) adds statutory layer — confusion in questions
Distinction from Sixth Schedule which has different amendment procedure (special majority needed for some parts)

concepts.name: Sixth Schedule Amendments — Tribal Areas in Northeast
key_dimensions: Covers autonomous district councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram
Amendment requires simple majority — Parliament can alter the Schedule through ordinary legislation
Trap: Sixth Schedule areas are inside the state but have special governance — confusion with Fifth Schedule applicability
Judicial interpretation on extent of autonomy and Parliament's override power

concepts.name: Creation and Abolition of Legislative Councils — Article 169
key_dimensions: Parliament can create or abolish State Legislative Councils by simple majority if State Assembly passes resolution by special majority
Trap: State Assembly needs special majority (2/3 + majority) but Parliament needs only simple majority
This is a constitutional amendment affecting a state's legislature but NOT under Article 368
Recent examples: Andhra Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir — controversies around council abolition

concepts.name: Union Territories: Creation, Modification, Abolition
key_dimensions: Parliament can by simple majority create, modify, or abolish Union Territories under Article 3 read with First Schedule
Jammu & Kashmir reorganisation (2019): J&K converted to UT by simple majority — major UPSC-relevant example
Trap: Ladakh carved out as UT without legislature — Parliament's plenary power over UTs vs states
Distinction: UT with legislature (Delhi, Puducherry) vs without legislature — both created/abolished by simple majority

concepts.name: Citizenship Provisions — Articles 5–11 and Citizenship Act
key_dimensions: Article 11 explicitly empowers Parliament to regulate citizenship by ordinary legislation — simple majority
Citizenship Amendment Act 2019 amended Citizenship Act 1955 by simple majority — not a constitutional amendment
Trap: Confusing CAA 2019 (ordinary law) with constitutional amendment; CAA challenged under Article 14 not Article 368
Parliament's plenary power on citizenship vs state's lack of any role — federal asymmetry

concepts.name: Election Laws — Representation of the People Acts
key_dimensions: Articles 327 and 328 allow Parliament/State Legislature to make laws on elections by simple majority
Delimitation, reservation of seats, electoral rolls — all governed by ordinary legislation
Trap: Reservation of seats for SC/ST in Parliament (Article 334) requires Article 368 amendment to extend, but actual conduct of elections is simple majority
Recent changes: Election Laws (Amendment) Act 2021 — Aadhaar-voter ID linkage done by simple majority

concepts.name: Quorum and Procedural Rules of Parliament — Articles 100, 118
key_dimensions: Parliament can make rules of procedure by simple majority under Article 118
Quorum set at 1/10th of total membership under Article 100 — can be changed by simple majority
Anti-defection provisions (Tenth Schedule) require special majority to amend — trap vs ordinary procedural rules
Distinction: Constitutional rules requiring special majority vs parliamentary procedural rules (simple majority)

concepts.name: Salaries and Service Conditions of MPs — Article 106
key_dimensions: Article 106: salaries and allowances of members of Parliament determined by Parliament by law (simple majority)
Parliament (Members Emoluments) various Acts passed by simple majority — no constitutional amendment needed
Trap: MPs vote on their own salaries (no independent body) unlike judges whose salaries are in Second Schedule
Comparison: UK IPSA (Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority) vs India's self-regulation

concepts.name: Acquisition of Territory — Article 1 and Constitutional Practice
key_dimensions: Article 1 defines India's territory but Parliament can acquire foreign territory through executive action + simple majority legislation
100th Constitutional Amendment Act (2015) for Bangladesh land boundary — required Article 368 (special majority + state ratification) because it altered First Schedule
Trap: Territory acquisition vs territory cession — different constitutional requirements
Distinction between adding to First Schedule (special majority) vs administrative changes within existing territory (simple majority)

concepts.name: Delimitation and Readjustment of Constituencies — Article 82
key_dimensions: Parliament by law provides for delimitation after each census under Article 82 — simple majority
Delimitation Commission is statutory (not constitutional) body created by simple majority Delimitation Act
Trap: Delimitation Commission's orders have force of law and cannot be challenged in court — unusual finality for a statutory body
Freeze on delimitation until 2026 census (91st Amendment) — this freeze itself was a constitutional amendment (Article 368)

concepts.name: Jurisdiction and Powers of Supreme Court — Article 138
key_dimensions: Article 138 allows Parliament to extend SC's jurisdiction and powers by simple majority legislation
Distinction: Original jurisdiction under Article 131, appellate under 132-136 are constitutional — but additional jurisdiction is by statute
Trap: Parliament can expand but cannot curtail Supreme Court's constitutional jurisdiction by simple majority
Example: Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act — extended by ordinary law

concepts.name: Language Provisions — Article 343–351 and Official Languages Act
key_dimensions: Official Languages Act 1963 and its amendments passed by simple majority under Article 344(6)
Eighth Schedule languages can be added by simple majority — trap since it is a Schedule change
Trap: 8th Schedule amendments historically treated as simple majority but 100th, 92nd, 71st amendment acts used Article 368 — inconsistency in practice
Three-language formula, link language controversy — Parliament's role through ordinary legislation

concepts.name: Creation of New All-India Services — Article 312
key_dimensions: Article 312: Rajya Sabha can declare by 2/3 majority the need for new All-India Service — then Parliament creates by simple majority
Two-step process: Rajya Sabha special resolution (2/3 of members present and voting) + Parliament's ordinary law
Trap: The Rajya Sabha resolution requires 2/3 majority but the actual legislation creating the service is simple majority
No new All-India Service created since IFS (1966) — significance of federal safeguard through Rajya Sabha

concepts.name: Contingency Fund of India — Article 267
key_dimensions: Parliament by law determines the corpus of Contingency Fund — alterable by simple majority
Trap: Contingency Fund is established by Article 267 (constitutional) but its size/operation is by ordinary law
Similar provision for State Contingency Funds under Article 267(2) — State Legislature simple majority
Distinction from Consolidated Fund (Article 266) and Public Account — all constitutional but operational details by statute

concepts.name: Simple Majority vs Special Majority: UPSC Trap Zones and Overlaps
key_dimensions: Master trap: GST (101st Amendment) needed special majority + state ratification; but GST Council's procedures are by simple majority regulations
Anti-defection (10th Schedule) amendment needs special majority but Speaker's rulings under it need simple majority rules
Evolution test: How to identify if a provision needs simple vs special majority — presence in Article 368 list or explicit 'by law' clause in the Article itself
Comparative table trap: Gram Sabha (simple majority state law) vs Panchayat election (73rd Amendment, special majority) — institutional confusion
